newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels expand alternative government in east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Rebels expand alternative government in east Zaire.

text.p: Zaire abruptly agreed to a U.N. plan to halt a rebel war encroaching on its key military and economic centres, but guerrilla leaders scoffed at the move and extended alternative government in territory they control.

With rebels closing on its army's operational base in the northeastern city of Kisangani and advancing in the mining province of Shaba, Zaire called on Wednesday for international monitors to be sent.
President Mobutu Sese Seko's government said it wanted the urgent implementation of a U.N. peace plan it had dismissed last month as too timid.

"The president and the government demand the deployment, without delay, of an international monitoring force to implement the peace plan of (U.N. envoy) Mohammed Sahnoun," said the statement issued in the capital Kinshasa.
"It looks like Mobutu Sese Seko is just trying to find a way to back out because he is losing, and get the international community to protect him," said rebel justice minister Mwenze Kongolo.

Mwenze said the rebel leadership was more interested in setting up an administration in their territory, which now comprises a 1,000-km (600-mile) strip from the Rwandan and Ugandan borders in the east to the fringes of southern Shaba.

"What we are doing here in Kindu by setting up a new administration is more important. I cannot understand why the international community wants to protect Mobutu when everyone knows that the people want him to go," Mwenze told Reuters.
He was speaking after the installation of local university rector Lokombe Kitete as the new governor of Maniema Province, whose capital Kindu fell to the rebels at the weekend.

"We have to break away from the bad habits of the past, from corruption and theft," Kitete told reporters. "This region has been utterly neglected since Mobutu came to power in 1965. Now we can start to rebuild it."
Ethnic Tutsis initially launched an armed campaign last October to fight off attempts by local authorities to expel them to their ancestral homeland in Rwanda.

They are the spearhead of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire whose avowed objective is ending Mobutu's 31-year rule. The president is ailing in France and the army that has protected him is in disaray despite backing by European mercenaries.

The government statement said an international force would "verify on the spot the withdrawal of all foreign forces". Zaire accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of sending troops to help the rebels, a charge all three deny.
A regional military source said earlier that rebels were closing in on Kisangani and it could fall soon.
A February 18 U.N. Security Council resolution called for a truce, a pullout of all foreign troops including mercenaries with the army and respect for Zaire's territorial intergrity.
Zaire, which had preferred a French-backed plan for a U.N. intervention force, then described the resolution as timid.
Rebels say the only thing to be negotiated is how Mobutu will stand down and have resisted pressure for a ceasefire.
Mwenze said that himself, along with other members of a delegation from the rebel Alliance, had declined a scheduled appointment for talks in South Africa on Wednesday.
South African President Nelson Mandela threw his weight behind U.S.-backed secret talks in Cape Town last week but was unable to convince rebel chief Laurent Kabila to agree a truce.
